poems: Nine o'clock arrives with the confidence of someone who has not yet opened their email.

What I did yesterday.
What I will do today.
Blockers.
Blockers.
Blockers.
A badge flipped backward, photo against the ribs.

At 9:03 the second coffee stops being a habit
and becomes a decision.
The copier warming up like an animal that resents being touched.
Five minutes late is a personality.

Somewhere a nurse writes 0906 in a chart,
and that number will outlive everyone in the room.

Lift the tab.
Do not pierce the foil.
Wait for the machine to finish its noise.
A mug ring on a printed agenda.

9:09, and the plan for the day is still perfect,
because nothing has happened to it yet.

The meeting opens with someone asking if everyone can see the screen.
Everyone can see the screen.

You have already picked up your phone eleven times.
This is not a moral failing, only arithmetic.

A wheelbarrow parked mid-lawn,
committed to nothing.

9:13 a.m. is when the first lie of the day gets told,
usually about a deadline.

The mail truck idles. The driver eats something out of foil,
unhurried, four hours into it.
"Sorry, I was on mute. I said it looks fine."
Somebody's grandmother is at the bank, third in line, and content about it.
A pigeon working a parking lot with the patience of salaried labor.
Sync, n.: a meeting whose purpose is to schedule a second meeting.

If it is a school day, the kid who missed the bus
is riding up front now, silent, victorious.
In the stairwell, someone finishes crying and fixes their face.

Nine twenty-one.
Whatever you were going to do before work,
you have now not done.

The flag halyard clinks
outside the post office.
Somewhere it is 9:23 at night and a person is loading a dishwasher, thinking of nothing.

Enriched flour, sugar, palm oil, natural flavor.
Servings per container: about six.
You ate four.

The oldest unread message is from March.
It has become furniture.

A surveyor squints into a tripod
at nothing.

9:27. The dentist is running behind,
and so is everyone in the little room with the fish.
Two hours in, the roofer peels off one glove to answer the phone.

There is a version of this hour where the hard thing is already done.
It is not this one.
9:30 sharp, which in practice means 9:34.

A crossing guard, off duty until afternoon,
drinking coffee in a parked car.

Somebody's dog has already had the entire day
and is asleep on the good chair.
"No, keep going, my dog just wants to be on camera."

The pharmacy gate goes up.
Three people were already waiting,
all of them fine, all of them not.
A hospital band, cut off, left on the nightstand.

9:36. The week is quietly rescheduled
to begin tomorrow.

9:37. A phone rings three desks over.
Everyone develops perfect posture.

You will not remember this minute.
That was always the arrangement.
A ream of paper, still shrink-wrapped, propping a door.

If it is a school day, a class is doing long division.
Elsewhere, someone is hearing the word benign.

9:41. A highlighter dries mid-sentence,
taking the sentence with it.

9:42. The paint crew's tarp moves with the wind,
a slow gray lung.

Sign here.
Press hard, there are three copies,
and the last one is yours to lose.

New parents have been up for five hours
and are only now considered normal.
Quarter to ten, and the day has not been wasted yet, only spent.
A truck backing up somewhere behind everything, beeping, and nobody looks.

Drink water. Whatever is happening behind your eyes
started before the meeting, though the meeting will take credit.

9:48, and the printer needs a person,
which is the one thing it cannot print.

Somewhere an ultrasound wand goes cold against a belly
and the room agrees to be quiet.

9:50. A form asks for the same address
a third time.
A shopping cart parked in the farthest spot.

The barista knows the order and not the name.
This arrangement suits everyone.
"Can you hear me now. Can you hear me. Can you."

9:54. The meeting will end late because it began late,
a debt nobody restructures.

The desk recycling bin
receives one false start.

A school nurse re-reads the thermometer.
A phone tree is about to begin.
A shopping cart, far from its herd.
The hour is nearly out and the plan is still, technically, intact.

9:59. The meeting ends four minutes early
and nobody knows what to do with the winnings.
